proof_steps.text: Elementary cases and well-definedness. The empty multiset is ultra-tight (its images under zero-exchange sequences are empty, hence tight) and satisfies the displayed condition with $s=0$; for $r=1$ one has $L_1=\mathbb Z/\mathbb Z\cdot1=0$ by [F1], so $x_1-x_1=0$ for every occurrence, every finite multiset is tight, and no zero exchange exists because its defining equation reads $0-0=2$; thus every finite multiset in $L_1$ is ultra-tight and satisfies the condition with $s=0$. By [F1] the differences $x_k-x_l$ do not change when representatives are shifted by a multiple of $(1,\dots,1)$, so tightness and the zero-exchange steps are well defined on classes; a zero-exchange sequence may therefore be computed with any representatives. [F1, F2]

The reverse implication. Assume $s\in\mathbb Z^r$ satisfies the displayed condition. Replacing each occurrence $x\in X$ by $x-s$ (a bijection of $L_r$ by [F1]) we may assume $x_k-x_l\le1$ for all $x,k,l$; applying this to the pair $(l,k)$ gives $x_l-x_k\le1$, so $|x_k-x_l|\le1$ for all $x,k,l$. We prove by induction on the length of a zero-exchange sequence that every such multiset is tight, and suppress the shift by $s$ from the notation. Suppose the next exchange acts on $x,y\in X$ in coordinates $k,l$, so $(x_k-x_l)-(y_k-y_l)=2$. Since $x_k-x_l,y_k-y_l\in[-1,1]$, this forces $x_k-x_l=1$ and $y_k-y_l=-1$; writing $x'=x-e_k+e_l$ and $y'=y+e_k-e_l$, the coordinate differences of $x'$ are $x'_k-x'_l=-1$, and for $p\notin\{k,l\}$ we have $x'_k-x'_p=x_k-1-x_p\in[-1,1]$, $x'_p-x'_k=x_p-x_k+1\in[-1,1]$, $x'_l-x'_p=x_k-x_p\in[-1,1]$ and $x'_p-x'_l=x_p-x_l-1\in[-1,1]$, using $x_k=x_l+1$ and $|x_p-x_q|\le1$; the same computation with $y$ in place of $x$ and $y_l=y_k+1$ shows the same for $y'$. All other occurrences are unchanged and already have all coordinate differences in $[-1,1]$. Hence in every reachable multiset all coordinate differences lie in $[-1,1]$, and for any two occurrences $z,w$ of that multiset $(z_k-z_l)-(w_k-w_l)\le1-(-1)=2$: every reachable multiset is tight, so $X$ is ultra-tight. [F1, algebra]

Setup for the forward implication. Conversely assume $X$ ultra-tight; we prove by induction on $r$ that potentials $s\in\mathbb Z^r$ exist satisfying the displayed condition. The case $r=1$ is in step 1.1. Let $r\ge2$ and assume the result for $r-1$. Let $\pi\colon L_r\to L_{r-1}$ forget the last coordinate; every zero exchange in $\pi(X)$ in coordinates $k,l\le r-1$ lifts to the zero exchange in $X$ with the same coordinates and the same labelled occurrences, because the defining difference of the pair is unchanged; hence every zero-exchange sequence in $\pi(X)$ is the projection of one in $X$ and ends tight. So $\pi(X)$ is ultra-tight, and by induction there are integers $s_1,\dots,s_{r-1}$ with $x_k-x_l\le s_k-s_l+1$ for all $x\in X$ and $k,l\le r-1$; applying this to $(l,k)$ gives, with $a_{kl}:=s_k-s_l$, $\bigl|(x_k-x_l)-a_{kl}\bigr|\le1\qquad(k,l\le r-1).$ It remains to extend the potentials to the last coordinate: we must choose $s_r$ so that $|(x_k-x_r)-a_{kr}|\le1$ for all $x\in X$ and all $k\le r-1$, where now $a_{kr}=s_k-s_r$. It is enough to do this in the descending sequence of stages described below: at stage $t=r-1,\dots,1$ one adds the bounds for the single pair $(t,r)$ while keeping all bounds already proved for pairs with both entries $\le r-1$ or both entries $\ge t+1$. [F1, F2]

The stage $t=r-1$. Since $X$ is ultra-tight, the empty sequence shows that $X$ itself is tight; hence for all $x,y\in X$, $(x_{r-1}-x_r)-(y_{r-1}-y_r)\le2$ and, exchanging $x$ and $y$, $\ge-2$. The integers $x_{r-1}-x_r$ therefore have range at most $2$, so (choosing the integer midpoint) some integer $m$ satisfies $|(x_{r-1}-x_r)-m|\le1$ for all $x\in X$; choosing $s_r:=s_{r-1}-m$ gives $a_{r-1,r}=m$ and hence the pair-$(r-1,r)$ bound, while all bounds of step 2.1 with $k,l\le r-1$ are unchanged. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

Reduction to the exceptional case. Fix $t\le r-1$ and suppose the bounds $|(x_k-x_l)-a_{kl}|\le1$ are known for all $x\in X$ whenever $k,l\le r-1$ or $k,l\ge t+1$ (for $t=r-1$ this is step 3.1 together with step 2.1). We show that the bounds also hold for all pairs with $k,l\ge t$; as observed in step 2.1, the only new pair to control is $(t,r)$. If already $|(x_t-x_r)-a_{tr}|\le1$ for all $x$, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise some $x\in X$ has $x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2$ or $x_t-x_r\le a_{tr}-2$; replacing every occurrence $x$ by $-x$ and every $s_k$ by $-s_k$ (which preserves ultra-tightness and all current bounds by [F1]) we may assume the first case, so that for this $x$, $x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2 .$ [step 3.1, given]

Consequences of the choice of $x$, and the sandwich. For every $u\in\{t+1,\dots,r-1\}$ the known bounds give $x_t-x_u\le a_{tu}+1$ and $x_u-x_r\le a_{ur}+1$, so $x_t-x_r=(x_t-x_u)+(x_u-x_r)\le a_{tu}+a_{ur}+2=a_{tr}+2$; together with the choice of $x$ this forces equality throughout: $x_t-x_u=a_{tu}+1,\qquad x_u-x_r=a_{ur}+1\qquad(t<u<r).$ Tightness against $x$ gives $y_t-y_r\ge a_{tr}$; choosing any $t<u<r$ and adding the old upper bounds for $(t,u)$ and $(u,r)$ gives $y_t-y_r\le a_{tr}+2$. Thus $a_{tr}\le y_t-y_r\le a_{tr}+2\qquad\text{for every }y\in X .$ [step 4.1, algebra]

The graph, the basic lower bound, and the case of no path. Draw a directed graph $G$ on $\{1,\dots,r\}$ with an arrow $k\to l$ if and only if some $y\in X$ satisfies $y_k-y_l=a_{kl}-1$. First we note that $x_k-x_r\ge a_{kr}+1\qquad\text{for every }k<r:$ for $k=u\ge t+1$ this is the equality $x_u-x_r=a_{ur}+1$ of step 5.1, for $k=t$ it follows from $x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2$, and for $k<t$ it follows from $x_k-x_r=(x_k-x_t)+(x_t-x_r)\ge (a_{kt}-1)+(a_{tr}+2)=a_{kr}+1$ using the known bound for the pair $(k,t)$ with $k,t\le r-1$. Suppose first that $G$ contains no directed path from $t$ to $r$. Let $T$ be the set of vertices reachable from $t$ (so $t\in T$, $r\notin T$) and let $R$ be its complement; there is no arrow from $T$ to $R$, since such an arrow would put its target in $T$. Define new potentials $\hat s_k:=s_k+1$ for $k\in T$ and $\hat s_k:=s_k$ for $k\in R$, and set $\hat a_{kl}:=\hat s_k-\hat s_l$. Then $\hat a_{tr}=a_{tr}+1,\qquad \hat a_{kl}\in\{a_{kl}-1,a_{kl},a_{kl}+1\},$ and $\hat a_{kl}=a_{kl}-1$ occurs exactly for $k\in R$, $l\in T$. The new $(t,r)$ bound follows from the sandwich of step 5.1: $\hat a_{tr}-1=a_{tr}\le y_t-y_r\le a_{tr}+2=\hat a_{tr}+1$ for all $y\in X$. For any other pair the bound is immediate if $\hat a_{kl}\ge a_{kl}$, since the old upper bound $y_k-y_l\le a_{kl}+1\le\hat a_{kl}+1$ survives. If $\hat a_{kl}=a_{kl}-1$, then $k\in R$, $l\in T$; the absence of an arrow from $T$ to $R$ says no $y$ has $y_l-y_k=a_{lk}-1$, so the old lower bound $y_l-y_k\ge a_{lk}-1$ improves to $y_l-y_k\ge a_{lk}$ for all $y$, i.e. $y_k-y_l\le -a_{lk}=a_{kl}=\hat a_{kl}+1$. Thus the bounds hold for all pairs with both entries in $\{t,\dots,r\}$, as required, and stage $t$ is complete in the no-path case. [step 5.1, algebra]

The case of a path: the witnesses. Now suppose $G$ contains a directed path from $t$ to $r$, and let $t=k_1\to k_2\to\cdots\to k_h=r$ be one of minimal length (so $k_1,\dots,k_h$ are pairwise distinct by [F2]). For each $m=1,\dots,h-1$ choose an occurrence $y_m\in X$ witnessing the arrow $k_m\to k_{m+1}$, i.e. $y_{m,k_m}-y_{m,k_{m+1}}=a_{k_mk_{m+1}}-1$, Distinct edges have distinct witnessing occurrences. Indeed, for any witness put $z=y-s$. The first $r-1$ coordinates have spread at most one. A witness for two edges ending before $r$ would have the same low value at both starts and the same high value at both ends, giving a shortcut from the earlier start to the later end. For a last-edge witness, $z_{k_{h-1}}=z_r-1$; tightness against the chosen $x$ and step 6.1 give $z_k-z_r\ge-1$ for $k<r$, and the old spread bound gives $z_k-z_r\le0$. If it also witnessed an earlier edge, that edge would start at $z_r-1$, giving a shortcut directly to $r$. Both contradict shortestness. Now put $x^{(m)}:=x-e_{k_{m+1}}+e_r\qquad(1\le m<h),$ so that $x^{(h-1)}=x$ because $k_h=r$. We shall prove by downward induction on $m$ that there is a multiset $Y_m\equiv X$ (in the equivalence relation generated by zero exchanges) containing $x^{(m)}$ and every occurrence among $y_1,\dots,y_m$ other than the chosen moving occurrence $x$, and that the following two statements hold: $B_m:\quad (x^{(m)}_{k_m}-x^{(m)}_{k_{m+1}})-(y_{m,k_m}-y_{m,k_{m+1}})=2, \qquad C_m:\quad x_{k_m}-x_r=a_{k_m r}+1 .$ Reading $C_1$ together with step 4.1 (which gives $x_{k_1}-x_r=x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2$) will then contradict the choice of $x$; the contradiction is completed below. We record $B_{h-1}$ and $C_{h-1}$: by the basic lower bound of step 6.1, $(x_{k_{h-1}}-x_r)-(y_{h-1,k_{h-1}}-y_{h-1,r})\ge(a_{k_{h-1}r}+1)-(a_{k_{h-1}r}-1)=2$, while tightness of $Y_{h-1}:=X$ gives $\le2$; hence equality holds, which is $B_{h-1}$, and then $C_{h-1}$ follows because $y_{h-1,k_{h-1}}-y_{h-1,r}=a_{k_{h-1}r}-1$ and $(x_{k_{h-1}}-x_r)-(y_{h-1,k_{h-1}}-y_{h-1,r})=2$. [step 6.1, given]

The induction step constructing $Y_m$. Let $m\le h-2$ and assume $A_{m+1}$ and $B_{m+1}$, where $A_{m+1}$ says that $Y_{m+1}\equiv X$ contains $x^{(m+1)}$ and every $y_j$ with $j\le m+1$ other than the original moving occurrence $x$. Form $Y_m$ from $Y_{m+1}$ by removing the occurrences $x^{(m+1)}$ and $y_{m+1}$ and adding the occurrences $x^{(m)}$ and $y_{m+1}+e_{k_{m+1}}-e_{k_{m+2}}$. By $B_{m+1}$ the pair $\bigl(x^{(m+1)},y_{m+1}\bigr)$ has difference exactly $2$ in coordinates $(k_{m+1},k_{m+2})$, so this is a zero exchange; hence $Y_m\equiv Y_{m+1}\equiv X$ by $A_{m+1}$, and the distinctness of the edge witnesses ensures that $Y_m$ retains every $y_j$ with $j\le m$ other than the original moving occurrence $x$, together with $x^{(m)}$. Thus $A_m$ holds. [step 7.1, algebra]

The induction step forcing $B_m$ and $C_m$, and the contradiction. Let $m\le h-2$ and assume $A_m$ and $C_{m+1}$. The witness $y_m$ cannot be the original moving occurrence $x$: its edge equation together with $C_{m+1}$ would give $x_{k_m}-x_r=(a_{k_mk_{m+1}}-1)+(a_{k_{m+1}r}+1)=a_{k_mr}$, contradicting step 6.1. Thus $y_m$ is retained in $Y_m$ by $A_m$. Since $k_1,\dots,k_h$ are pairwise distinct and only $k_h$ equals $r$, the $r$-th coordinate of $e_r$ vanishes in positions $k_m$ and $k_{m+1}$, so $x^{(m)}_{k_m}-x^{(m)}_{k_{m+1}} =(x_{k_m}-x_r)-(x_{k_{m+1}}-x_r)+1 \ge (a_{k_m r}+1)-(a_{k_{m+1}r}+1)+1 =a_{k_mk_{m+1}}+1 =y_{m,k_m}-y_{m,k_{m+1}}+2,$ where the inequality uses the basic lower bound of step 6.1 for $k_m$ and statement $C_{m+1}$ for $k_{m+1}$. Since $Y_m$ is tight (it lies in the class of the ultra-tight $X$), the reverse inequality holds and we have equality, which is $B_m$; reading the equality back through the displayed chain gives $x_{k_m}-x_r=a_{k_m r}+1$, which is $C_m$. Downward induction on $m$ now gives $C_1$, i.e. $x_{k_1}-x_r=x_t-x_r=a_{tr}+1$, contradicting $x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2$ from the choice of $x$ in step 4.1. Hence the exceptional case cannot occur: with the current potentials the pair $(t,r)$ is already bounded, so stage $t$ is complete in the path case as well. [step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra]

Completion of the induction. Stages $t=r-1,r-2,\dots,1$ have now been treated: each stage either leaves the potentials unchanged, or (in the no-path case of step 6.1) replaces them by potentials for which the new bound holds, while all bounds proved earlier are preserved (the modification changes $s_k-s_l$ by at most $1$ in the necessary direction, and the argument of step 6.1 checks both the improved and the unchanged pairs). After stage $1$ the bounds hold for all pairs $k,l$ with $k,l\le r-1$ or $k,l\ge1$, i.e. for all $k,l\in\{1,\dots,r\}$. This proves the forward implication for $r$, and with the base case $r=1$ of step 1.1 and the induction scheme of step 2.1, the forward implication for all $r\ge1$. Combined with the reverse implication of step 1.2, an ultra-tight multiset is exactly one admitting column potentials $s$, including the empty multiset and the case $r=1$. [step 1.1, step 6.1, step 9.1] ∎

proof_steps.text: Ordered spanning without localization. For every $f\in P$ the presentation relations give $T_if=s_i(f)T_i+c_{i,i+1}(f-s_i(f))$, where $c_{i,i+1}=(z-1)X_{i+1}/(X_{i+1}-X_i)$. The correction is in $P$: $f-s_i(f)$ is divisible by $X_{i+1}-X_i$, first for ordinary monomials by the difference-of-powers identity, and then for Laurent monomials after multiplying by a symmetric Laurent monomial unit. For $f=X_i$ this is the Bernstein relation, for $f=X_{i+1}$ it is its conjugate using the quadratic relation, and the general formula follows by addition and the product rule $f g-s_i(f g)=(f-s_i(f))g+s_i(f)(g-s_i(g))$, including inverse generators by applying that rule to $f f^{-1}=1$. Moving a polynomial across a $T$ reduces the number of misplaced polynomial factors, and correction terms reduce the number of $T$ factors; the finite Hecke relations then span the remaining words by $T_w$. Thus $H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}$ is spanned over $P$ by the $T_w$, and the presentation anti-involution fixing $X_i,T_i$ gives right ordered spanning too. [F1, F2, algebra]

A representation of the unlocalized presentation. Form $K\rtimes S_n$ with multiplication $(f\sigma)(g\tau)=f\sigma(g)\sigma\tau$. For distinct indices set $c_{ij}=(z-1)X_j/(X_j-X_i)$ and $d_{ij}=(X_j-zX_i)/(X_j-X_i)=z-c_{ij}$, and assign $T_i\mapsto c_{i,i+1}+d_{i,i+1}s_i$, $X_j\mapsto X_j$. The rational identities $c_{ij}+c_{ji}=z-1$ and $d_{ij}d_{ji}=z+(z-1)c_{ij}-c_{ij}^2$ give the quadratic relation. For three distinct indices, expansion of the two braid products in their six permutation coefficients agrees: the longest coefficients are $d_{ij}d_{ik}d_{jk}$ in either order; the two length-two coefficients agree by commuting scalar factors; the length-one and identity coefficients agree using $c_{ij}c_{jk}=c_{ik}(c_{ij}+c_{jk}-(z-1))$ together with the preceding quadratic identities. These identities follow by multiplying by the common product of the differences and expanding the polynomial numerators. Distant relations follow from disjoint variable pairs. Finally $T_if-s_i(f)T_i=c_{i,i+1}(f-s_i(f))$, so the Bernstein and mixed relations hold. All denominators here are nonzero polynomials in independent variables in the domain $P$. This defines a homomorphism from the unlocalized presented algebra to $K\rtimes S_n$. [F1, algebra]

Localization and intertwiners. Let $S$ be the multiplicative set generated by all $X_i-X_j$ with $i\ne j$. It is invariant under $S_n$. The mixed formula of step 1.1 extends to $S^{-1}P$ by the same product rule and by solving the formula for inverses of elements of $S$; the correction remains in $S^{-1}P$. Consequently adjoining these inverses gives the algebra with free left coefficient module $\bigoplus_w(S^{-1}P)T_w$ and the same multiplication rules. This realizes the localization: the inverse formulas make it universal among homomorphisms inverting $S$, and its injective representation in $K\rtimes S_n$ follows from the identical maximal-length argument of step 1.3. In it put $\Phi_i=T_i-c_{i,i+1}$; the mixed formula gives $\Phi_if=s_i(f)\Phi_i$ for all $f\in S^{-1}P$. Products $\Phi_w$ along reduced words have unitriangular expansions in the $T_v$, because selecting every $T$ gives $T_w$ and selecting any scalar correction leaves strictly shorter words; thus they too form a basis over $S^{-1}P$. No parameter difference $U_a-U_b$, quantum factorial or Gram determinant is inverted. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

Polynomial multiplication is injective over the universal domain. If $0\ne f\in P$ and $h=\sum_w f_wT_w$, then $fh=0$ gives $ff_w=0$ for each $w$ by step 1.3. Since $P$ is a domain, every $f_w=0$, so $h=0$. The right-basis argument gives the analogous right multiplication result. This injectivity assertion is over the universal domain, as in Statement (2), and does not assert injectivity of nonzero zero divisors after arbitrary base change. [step 1.3, algebra]

Subword support in the localization. Expanding a reduced product $T_w=\prod_t(\Phi_{i_t}+c_{i_t,i_t+1})$ and moving coefficients left using step 2.1 gives terms supported on products of subwords of the reduced word. Every coefficient is a sum of products of permuted $c$ functions and hence has only variable-difference denominators. Equivalently, in the crossed product $\Phi_i=d_{i,i+1}s_i$, so moving a localized polynomial $f$ through such a term replaces it by the corresponding subword permutation applied to $f$. This proves the subword expansion used by consumers and the asserted intertwining throughout the embedded localization. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

Conclusion. Step 1.3 proves both ordered bases over $R$ and after arbitrary base change with unit $z$; step 2.2 proves the universal-domain injectivity; and steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the localized embedding and intertwining identity. For $n=0$ there are no polynomial or Hecke generators, $S_0$ consists of the identity, the lone ordered monomial is $1$, and $H_0^{\mathrm{aff}}=R$; all localization and intertwining clauses are then vacuous. No cyclotomic basis, trace form, primitive-content assertion or Brundan–Kleshchev result is used. [step 1.3, step 2.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

proof_steps.text: Elementary straightening of polynomials past a simple generator. In the nondegenerate branch the mixed relation gives, for a polynomial $p$ in the commuting variables, $T_rp=(s_rp)T_r-(q_H-1)X_{r+1}\frac{p-s_rp}{X_r-X_{r+1}},$ and in the degenerate branch $s_rp=(s_rp)s_r-\frac{p-s_rp}{x_r-x_{r+1}} .$ Both divided differences are polynomials: for $p=X_r^m$ the first identity is $T_rX_r^m=X_{r+1}^mT_r-(q_H-1)(X_r^{m-1}+X_r^{m-2}X_{r+1}+\dots+X_{r+1}^{m-1})X_{r+1}$, which follows from [F1] by induction on $m$, and the second is $s_rx_r^m=x_{r+1}^ms_r-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}x_r^kx_{r+1}^{m-1-k}$, again by induction; the general case follows from the divided-difference product rule for the two variable replacements $X_r\leftrightarrow X_{r+1}$ and $x_r\leftrightarrow x_{r+1}$. Consequently any word in the generators and polynomial variables rewrites as an $A$-linear combination of ordered monomials $X^aT_w$ in the nondegenerate branch (the $T$-word reduced by [F2], polynomial factors collected by commutation) and of $x^aw$ in the degenerate branch. The nondegenerate straightening preserves total polynomial degree; the degenerate one lowers degree by one in the correction term. [F1, F2, algebra]

The nondegenerate quotient is generated by positive powers. In the nondegenerate branch the relation $f(X_1)=0$ has nonzero constant term $a_0$, so $X_1^{-1}=-a_0^{-1}(X_1^{\ell-1}+a_{\ell-1}X_1^{\ell-2}+\dots+a_1)$ is a polynomial in $X_1$; and from $T_rX_rT_r=q_HX_{r+1}$ one gets $X_{r+1}^{-1}=q_HT_r^{-1}X_r^{-1}T_r^{-1}$ by inverting the equation. Starting from the displayed polynomial expression for $X_1^{-1}$ and iterating this forward recursion expresses every $X_r^{-1}$ through positive powers of $X_1$ and the $T$'s, since $T_r^{-1}=q_H^{-1}(T_r-q_H+1)$ is a polynomial in $T_r$. Therefore the quotient is already generated, as an $A$-module, by words in $X_1,\dots,X_d$ and the $T_r$, and step 1.1 applies to them. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

The transported relations in the nondegenerate branch. Put $R_1:=f(X_1)$ and $R_{r+1}:=T_rR_rT_r$; each $R_r$ is zero in the quotient. We claim by induction on $r$ that ordered straightening writes $R_r=q_H^{r-1}X_r^{\ell}+\sum_{a,w}c_{a,w}X_1^{a_1}\cdots X_r^{a_r}T_w,$ where $w\in S_r$, $\sum_ja_j\le\ell$, $a_r<\ell$, and no variable of index above $r$ occurs. The case $r=1$ is the definition, with constant coefficient rearranged. For the induction step, direct summation of the mixed relation gives, for $m\ge1$, $T_rX_r^mT_r=q_HX_{r+1}^m-(q_H-1)\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}X_r^kX_{r+1}^{m-k}T_r,$ and for $m=0$ one uses $T_r^2=(q_H-1)T_r+q_H$. Transporting the leading term $q_H^{r-1}X_r^{\ell}$ therefore produces exactly $q_H^rX_{r+1}^{\ell}$ plus terms of $X_{r+1}$-degree below $\ell$. Each remainder monomial has $X_r$-degree $a_r<\ell$; variables of index below $r$ commute with $T_r$ and with $X_{r+1}$, and $T_w\in H_r$ for $w\in S_r$, so applying the displayed formula to $X_r^{a_r}$ and then straightening the finite words $T_rT_wT_r$, $T_wT_r$ by [F2] produces terms of $X_{r+1}$-degree at most $a_r<\ell$ and total polynomial degree at most $\ell$. This proves the claim. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

The transported relations in the degenerate branch. Put $R_1:=f(x_1)$ and $R_{r+1}:=s_rR_rs_r$. Straightening and induction on $r$ show $R_r=x_r^{\ell}+\sum_{a,w}c_{a,w}x^aw,$ where $w\in S_r$, all occurring variables have index at most $r$, and $\sum_ja_j<\ell$: conjugation transports $x_r^m$ by $s_rx_r^ms_r=x_{r+1}^m-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}x_r^kx_{r+1}^{m-1-k}s_r,$ so the leading term $x_r^{\ell}$ produces $x_{r+1}^{\ell}$ plus correction terms of total degree $\ell-1$, and every old remainder, when straightened, stays of degree below $\ell$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

Termination of the nondegenerate reduction. Order exponent vectors lexicographically as $(a_d,a_{d-1},\dots,a_1)$, larger first differing coordinate larger; this is a well-order on $\mathbb N^d$ preserved by addition. Suppose $a_r\ge\ell$ for some $r$ and some spanning monomial $X^aT_w$. Multiplying the zero relation $R_r$ of step 2.2 on the left by $X^{a-\ell e_r}$ and on the right by $T_w$ gives a relation whose leading term is $q_H^{r-1}X^aT_w$ and whose remaining terms all have the same coordinates above $r$ and a strictly smaller $r$-th coordinate (increases in coordinates below $r$ do not affect the lexicographic comparison), with $w\in S_r$ and finite straightening changing no dot exponents. Hence the bounded ordered monomials span the nondegenerate quotient, over $A$ and after any base change. [step 2.2, algebra]

Termination of the degenerate reduction. If $a_r\ge\ell$, multiply the zero relation $R_r$ of step 2.3 on the left by $x^{a-\ell e_r}$ and on the right by $w$; the leading term is $x^aw$, and every other term has total degree strictly below $\sum_ja_j$ (all other coefficients come from the remainder of $R_r$, of degree $<\ell$). Induction on the total degree $\sum_ja_j$ therefore expresses every element in terms of monomials $x^aw$ with all $a_r<\ell$. This also shows that no relation $f(x_r)=0$ for $r>1$ is claimed: at level one $f(t)=t$, and $x_1=0$ gives $x_2=s_1$, which is exactly the form of the reduced spanning family. [step 2.3, algebra]

Conclusion. The specialisations $f(t)=\prod_i(t-q_H^i)^{\lambda_i}$ and $f(t)=\prod_i(t-i)^{\lambda_i}$ are instances of the two branches with $\ell=\sum_i\lambda_i$. For $\ell=0$ the imposed relation is $1=0$, giving the zero algebra for $d>0$ and $A$ for $d=0$, as stated. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

proof_steps.text: The operator model. Let $S_r$ be the automorphism of $K$ swapping $z_r,z_{r+1}$ and fixing the other variables, and put $\delta_r:=z_r-z_{r+1}$. Let $z_j$ act on $K$ by multiplication and let $A_r:=S_r+\frac{S_r-1}{\delta_r}=\Bigl(1+\frac1{\delta_r}\Bigr)S_r-\frac1{\delta_r}.$ For $p\in P$ the difference $S_rp-p$ is divisible by $\delta_r$ in $P$ (write $p$ in the variables $z_r,z_{r+1}$ with the remaining variables as scalars and use that $z_r^az_{r+1}^b-z_{r+1}^az_r^b$ is divisible by $\delta_r$), so $A_r$ preserves $P$; hence the operators $z_j$ (multiplication) and $A_r$ generate a subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}_F(K)$ and, restricted to $P$, of $\operatorname{End}_F(P)$. [given, construct]

Verification of the defining relations in the model. Direct substitution gives the mixed relations $A_rz_r-z_{r+1}A_r=-1$, $A_rz_{r+1}-z_rA_r=1$, and $A_rz_j=z_jA_r$ for $j\notin\{r,r+1\}$. Writing $a(t):=1+1/t$ and $b(t):=-1/t$, so that $A_r=a(\delta_r)S_r+b(\delta_r)$, and using $S_r(\delta_r)=-\delta_r$, the identity coefficient of $A_r^2$ is $a(\delta_r)a(-\delta_r)+b(\delta_r)^2=1$ and its $S_r$-coefficient is $a(\delta_r)b(-\delta_r)+b(\delta_r)a(\delta_r)=0$, so $A_r^2=1$; distant $A_r$ commute because their permutations and coefficients involve disjoint variable pairs. For the braid relation put $u:=z_r-z_{r+1}$, $v:=z_{r+1}-z_{r+2}$, $w:=u+v=z_r-z_{r+2}$, $S:=S_r$, $T:=S_{r+1}$; expanding $A_rA_{r+1}A_r$ and $A_{r+1}A_rA_{r+1}$ in $K\rtimes S_d$ gives the six permutation coefficients $-\frac{uv+1}{uvw}\ (1),\quad \frac{a(u)}{vw}\ (S),\quad \frac{a(v)}{uw}\ (T),\quad -\frac{a(u)a(w)}{v}\ (ST),\quad -\frac{a(v)a(w)}{u}\ (TS),\quad a(u)a(w)a(v)\ (STS),$ and the right expansion has the same six coefficients with $u,v$ and $S,T$ interchanged, so the two expansions agree. These are rational identities valid in every characteristic, including $2$. Hence the assignment $z_j\mapsto$ multiplication by $z_j$, $s_r\mapsto A_r$ defines an algebra homomorphism $H_d^{\deg}\to\operatorname{End}_F(K)$ (and into $\operatorname{End}_F(P)$ by step 1.1). [F1, algebra]

Spanning. In the model, $s_rp=(S_rp)s_r-(p-S_rp)\delta_r^{-1}$ for every polynomial $p$, so every word in the generators rewrites as a linear combination of the ordered monomials $z^aw$ with $a_j\ge0$ and $w\in S_d$, the power-polynomial part being collected by commutativity and the $s$-word reduced by [F2]. The same straightening performed in $H_d^{\deg}$ (available there because the model satisfies the defining relations, or by the same elementary computation in the presentation) shows that the ordered monomials span the algebra. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

Independence. In the crossed-product expansion of a reduced product $A_w$, the coefficient at $w$ is $c_w=\prod_{k=1}^{m}(1+1/(s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_{k-1}})(\delta_{i_k}))\ne0$; every other permutation has length less than $\ell(w)$, because it is represented by a proper subword. The distinct field automorphisms are independent over $K$: from a shortest nonzero operator relation $\sum_jf_j\sigma_j=0$, compose with multiplication by a variable on which some $\sigma_j$ differs from $\sigma_1$, and subtract the original relation multiplied by $\sigma_1$ of that variable. This gives a shorter nonzero relation; a one-term relation cannot annihilate $1$. Thus the crossed product acts faithfully on $K$. Now an $F$-linear relation among the ordered monomials maps to $\sum_w f_w(z)A_w=0$, with $f_w(z)=\sum_a c_{a,w}z^a\in P$. If some $f_w$ is nonzero, choose such a $w$ of maximal length. Its coefficient is $f_wc_w\ne0$ and receives no contribution from any other maximal-length label or shorter label, a contradiction. Therefore every $f_w=0$, and polynomial coefficient uniqueness gives every $c_{a,w}=0$. This proves $F$-linear independence of the ordered monomials, without asserting their impossible $K$-linear independence. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

Conclusion. Steps 3.1 and 2.1 show that the family $\{x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_d^{a_d}w:a_j\ge0,\ w\in S_d\}$ both spans and is linearly independent in $H_d^{\deg}$ over $F$; renaming the commuting generators $z_j\mapsto x_j$ and using the presentation [F1] gives the asserted $F$-basis. No cyclotomic quotient, BK isomorphism or dimension theorem is used, and for $d=0$ the family consists of the empty monomial alone. [step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

proof_steps.text: Beta sets, bead moves and the rim-hook dictionary. By [F1] a bead move $u\mapsto u-h$ with $u\in B$, $u-h\notin B$ unwraps a rim hook of length $h$ whose foot has residue $u-h+1$ modulo $e$: if $\beta_i=u$ and $\beta_j<u-h<\beta_{j-1}$, the rows $i,\dots,j-1$ change by the boundary between those two beta positions, the lost border strip has $h$ boxes, and its lowest-row leftmost lost column makes the foot content $u-h+1$; reversing the move wraps a hook with foot residue the starting beta position plus one. Moving a bead one position upward on its runner therefore removes an $e$-hook, and packing every runner upward leaves the number of beads relative to the negative reference tail on each runner unchanged; by [F2] the result is the componentwise $e$-core independent of the order. Every $e$-hook contains one node of each residue, so hook removal preserves the hub (the residue-count vector modulo the all-one vector) and subtracts the all-one vector from the residue counts. [F1, F2, algebra]

The boundary-count identity. Let $C_i$ be the residue counts and $\delta_i$ the number of removable minus addable $i$-nodes. We prove $\delta_i=2C_i-C_{i-1}-C_{i+1}-m_i$ by induction while adjoining nodes to the empty multipartition. The empty multipartition has $C_i=0$ for all $i$ and $\delta_i=-m_i$ (each component contributes one addable first node of its residue $c_a$ in the empty diagram), which gives the identity initially. Adjoining a node of residue $j$ changes the boundary count by $+2$ at $j$ and $-1$ at each of $j-1$ and $j+1$ (counted twice when $e=2$); these changes are read off by recording the occupied and vacant beta positions before and after the corresponding one-position bead move, all other adjacent occupancies cancelling. The right-hand side changes in exactly the same way because $C_j$ increases by $1$ and $C_i$ for $i\ne j$ is unchanged. Induction on the number of nodes gives the identity for every multipartition. [F1, algebra]

Cores and their height matrices. For a componentwise $e$-core let $b_{ia}$ be the largest bead on runner $i$ ($0\le i<e$) and $t_{ia}=(b_{ia}-i)/e$, so the packed beta set on runner $i$ is $\{i+ek:k\le t_{ia}\}$. Counting beads $\ge-eL$ for large $L$ gives the column sums $\sum_i t_{ia}=c_a-e$. Writing $R_i=\sum_at_{ia}$, the hub satisfies $\delta_i=R_i-R_{i-1}$ for $1\le i<e$ and $\delta_0=R_0-R_{e-1}-\ell$; since $\sum_iR_i=\sum_ac_a-e\ell$ is fixed, equal hub is equivalent to equal row sums. Hence cores of a fixed hub and fixed charges are exactly the integer $e\times\ell$ matrices $T=(t_{ia})$ with fixed row sums $R_i$ and column sums $c_a-e$. [F1, F2, algebra]

Switches and energy. Let $T$ be an integer $e\times\ell$ matrix with fixed margins, and consider a switch in distinct rows $i,j$ and distinct columns $a,b$, replacing $(t_{ia},t_{ib},t_{ja},t_{jb})$ by $(t_{ia}-1,t_{ib}+1,t_{ja}+1,t_{jb}-1)$; margins are preserved. With $\gamma:=t_{ia}-t_{ib}-t_{ja}+t_{jb}$, the squared-norm changes by $4-2\gamma$: so $\gamma=2$ is a zero-energy switch and $\gamma\ge3$ strictly lowers the energy. Regard the $e$ labelled rows of $T$ as a multiset in $L_\ell=\mathbb Z^\ell/\mathbb Z(1,\dots,1)$; it is tight exactly when $\gamma\le2$ for all choices, and switches with $\gamma=2$ are exactly the zero exchanges of [F3]. [F3, algebra]

Equal hub and equal size give equal content. If two multipartitions have equal hubs, the difference $d_i$ of their residue counts satisfies $2d_i-d_{i-1}-d_{i+1}=0$ by step 1.2, because the $\delta_i$ and $m_i$ terms are unchanged; hence all first differences $d_i-d_{i-1}$ are equal, and summing them around the cycle makes this common difference $0$, so $d$ is constant. Therefore equal hub and equal size imply equal content, and equal hubs imply sizes congruent modulo $e$. [step 1.2, algebra]

The size formula. If $T(\kappa),T(\eta)$ are the height matrices of two such cores, then $|\eta|-|\kappa|=\frac e2\Bigl(\sum_{i,a}t_{ia}(\eta)^2-\sum_{i,a}t_{ia}(\kappa)^2\Bigr).$ Indeed, count the beta numbers $\ge-eL$ in a component: their number is $eL+c_a$, the same for both cores, while their sum changes by $\sum_i i\,\Delta t_{ia}+\frac e2\sum_i\Delta(t_{ia}^2+t_{ia})$; from $\beta_j=\lambda_j+c_a-j$ the change in that sum equals the change in the partition size, and summing over $a$ the equal row sums kill $\sum_i i\sum_a\Delta t_{ia}$ while the equal column sums kill the linear $\sum\Delta t_{ia}$ term. In particular the squared-norm difference is even, so the displayed size difference is an integer multiple of $e$. [F1, step 1.3, algebra]

Ultra-tight rows and the global minimum. If the row multiset is not ultra-tight, a finite sequence of zero switches leads to a non-tight matrix, at which some rows and columns have $\gamma\ge3$, giving a strict descent: every intermediate matrix has the same margins, zero switches preserve core size by step 2.2, and a strict descent lowers core size by $e(\gamma-2)\ge e$. If instead the multiset is ultra-tight, [F3] supplies a column potential $s_a$ with every row of $U=(t_{ia}-s_a)$ having maximum minus minimum at most one. For a fixed row sum such a row minimizes the sum of squares over all integer rows: if two entries differ by at least $2$, transferring one from the larger to the smaller lowers the square sum by at least $2$, and repeated transfers terminate; the minimum is attained exactly by rows whose entries differ by at most one. Column potentials do not affect comparisons of total squared norm between matrices with the same column sums, because $\sum_{i,a}(t_{ia}-s_a)^2=\sum_{i,a}t_{ia}^2-2\sum_as_a\sum_it_{ia}+e\sum_as_a^2 .$ Hence such a $T$ is a global minimum among the matrices of its margins, and conversely a global minimum admits no strict descent after zero switches, so its row multiset is ultra-tight. Starting from any $T$, repeated zero-path and strict-descent steps reach a global minimum, since all matrices represent genuine cores of nonnegative integer size and strict descent lowers that size by at least $e$; minima therefore exist for every nonempty fixed-hub class. [F3, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 1.4, algebra]

Equal-size connectivity of minima. Let $T,V$ be two global minima with the same margins, and let $s$ be the column potential of $T$ from step 3.1. Every row of $U=T-s$ is balanced, with entries $u_i$ or $u_i+1$; since $V-s$ has the same row sums and the same total energy, each of its rows also attains the row minimum and has entries $u_i$ or $u_i+1$. Subtracting $u_i$ from row $i$ produces two binary $e\times\ell$ matrices $A,B$ with identical row and column sums. If $A\ne B$, the difference $D=A-B$ has entries $0,\pm1$ and zero row and column sums; starting from a $+1$ and alternating a $-1$ in the same row with a $+1$ in the same column produces a shortest alternating cycle with distinct rows $i_0,\dots,i_{t-1}$ and columns $j_0,\dots,j_{t-1}$, where $D_{i_kj_k}=+1$ and $D_{i_kj_{k+1}}=-1$. If $t=2$, switch the rectangle in $A$ to agree with $B$ there. If $t>2$, inspect $A_{i_0j_{t-1}}$ and $B_{i_0j_{t-1}}$: if $A_{i_0j_{t-1}}=0$, switching the rectangle with rows $i_0,i_{t-1}$ and columns $j_0,j_{t-1}$ gives a binary $A'$ with strictly fewer discrepancies from $B$; if $B_{i_0j_{t-1}}=1$, the reverse switch on $B$ gives a binary $B'$ with strictly fewer discrepancies from $A$; if neither holds, $D_{i_0j_{t-1}}=+1$ and a shorter alternating cycle exists, contradicting minimality. Induction on the discrepancy count connects $A$ and $B$ by binary switches, all preserving margins. Lifting these binary switches back to $T$ gives switches with $\gamma=2$, hence equal core size by step 2.2, preserving the hub. [F3, step 3.1, algebra]

Conclusion. Step 1.2 proves the boundary-count identity $\delta_i=2C_i-C_{i-1}-C_{i+1}-m_i$ with the double edge at $e=2$, and step 2.1 shows that equal hub and equal size are equivalent to equal content. Steps 1.3 and 2.2 identify cores of fixed hub and charges with integer matrices of fixed margins and give the squared-norm size formula; step 3.1 provides a same-hub core-switch path that never increases size and strictly decreases it whenever the core is not of minimum size, with minima existing in every nonempty class; and step 4.1 connects any two minimum-size cores by equal-size switches. These are exactly the finite-$e$ descent and reduced-core connectivity facts consumed by the Lyle–Mathas max-weight argument, proved locally without importing weight nonnegativity or matrix-alignment inputs. [step 3.1, step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎

proof_steps.text: Rank decomposition. For fixed $d$, the corner idempotents $e(\beta,i)$ over all root components $\beta$ of height $d-1$ and colors $i$ are orthogonal and sum to $1_{B_d}$: each word has exactly one last color and one prefix root, so it lies in exactly one corner. The zero-corner case gives $B_de(\beta,i)=0$ and is included since its summand is zero. [F1, F3, algebra]

The mixed commutators at $v=1$. Forgetting the grading shifts in the same-color categorical decomposition gives $[E_i^{\mathrm{basic}},F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}]=h_i(\Lambda-\beta)\operatorname{Id}$ on the root component $\beta$; its positive identity summands contribute $h_i$ copies and its negative identity summands contribute the signed counterpart, so the integral $[h_i]_v$ specializes at $v=1$ to the integer $h_i$ with no division by $v-v^{-1}$. The unequal-color mixed relation gives $[E_i^{\mathrm{basic}},F_j^{\mathrm{basic}}]=0$ for $i\ne j$. Hence $[E,D]=\sum_i[E_i^{\mathrm{basic}},F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}] =\Bigl(\sum_ih_i(\Lambda-\beta)\Bigr)\operatorname{Id}$ on root component $\beta$. For affine type A every Cartan column sums to zero, including the double-edge matrix at $e=2$, so $\sum_ih_i(\Lambda-\beta)=\sum_i\lambda_i-\sum_j\beta_j\sum_ia_{ij}=\ell$ independently of $\beta$. Therefore $[E,D]=\ell\cdot\operatorname{Id}$, and since rank-zero restriction is zero, $EP_0=0$; expanding $[E,D^d]=d\ell D^{d-1}$ gives $EP_d=d\ell\,P_{d-1}$. [F2, algebra]

The Hom-norm recurrence. For finite graded projectives define $h$ as in [F4]; it is additive in both variables, unchanged by shifts, and descends to projective $K_0$ modulo $v-1$. Pairing distinct root blocks by zero and summing over a fixed rank, the ordinary first adjunction $F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}\dashv E_i^{\mathrm{basic}}$ gives $h(F_i^{\mathrm{basic}}P,Q)=h(P,E_i^{\mathrm{basic}}Q)$, hence $h(DP,Q)=h(P,EQ)$; all restricted modules remain finite projectives by [F3], so the recurrence stays inside the declared group. Combining with step 1.2, $h(P_d,P_d)=h(DP_{d-1},P_d)=h(P_{d-1},EP_d) =d\ell\,h(P_{d-1},P_{d-1}).$ [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

proof_steps.text: A faithful KLR calculation, before quotient. Use independent dots and the rational operators of the normalization supplier’s local crossing and braid calculations: equal crossings act by $D=(S-1)/(u-v)$ and unequal crossings by $Sc_{ij}$, where $c_{ij}=(1-p)/N_{ij}$ in DG or $(1-P)/N_{ij}$ in NG. The pair product is exactly $K_{ij}$ and the five braid computations give corrections $0,1,-1,u+w-2v$, with the specified braid order. Thus these operators satisfy the affine sign-modified KLR presentation. This representation is faithful for formal dot coefficients: moving dots right by the proved sliding rule, use quadratic relations to remove repeated simple reflections and braid relations to reduce each crossing word to a chosen reduced word plus shorter words. This terminates by length (and the finite Coxeter reduction at each fixed length), giving a spanning family $\psi_we(i)$. Its leading permutation coefficient is a product of nonzero $c_{ij}$ and of $1/(u-v)$ for equal pairs; proper subwords have smaller permutation length. Maximal-length comparison in the matrix crossed product therefore proves independence of the formal coefficients. Clearing finitely many temporary dot differences is legitimate in this faithful affine calculation. It does not assert faithfulness after taking the cyclotomic quotient. [F1, F2, algebra]

The mixed and quadratic computations. In the representation of step 1.1, the displayed inverse Hecke element $\psi N-p$ (DG) or $\psi N-P$ (NG) is literally $S(1-\widehat p)-\widehat p$ or $S(1-\widehat P)-\widehat P$ on every word. On unequal colours this follows by cancellation of the right coefficient $N$; on equal colours $\psi=D$ and $D N-1=H$ by the equality $H+1=(S+1)(-N/(u-v))$. The supplier’s full affine coefficient check gives the mixed relation $Hx_{r+1}-x_rH=1$ in DG, and $HX_rH=qX_{r+1}$ in NG, together with $H^2=1$ or $H^2=(q-1)H+q$. Alternatively the DG mixed constant on an unequal word is $(i_r-i_{r+1}+u-v)p=1$, and on an equal word it is $(u-v)+N=1$; in NG the same spectral substitution gives the stated mixed identity. Commuting dots, distant mixed relations and distant crossings follow because the operators involve disjoint pairs. By step 1.1 these are regular affine-KLR identities and hence evaluate in the nilpotent-dot quotient. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

All five Hecke braid patterns. Moving the generators of a word one at a time around $\tau$, using steps 1.2 and 1.3, gives $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ for every pair of words, hence for all $a,b$ by $R$-bilinearity; the pairing $(a,b)\mapsto\tau(ab)$ is associative and symmetric. Restricted-profile zero values. For $0\le j\le n$ let $U_j$ be the span of the PBW words whose dot entries above $j$ vanish, all finite permutations included. It is a right finite-Hecke module. Multiplying its dot part by any polynomial in $X_1,\dots,X_j$ stays in $U_j$: transport the first cyclotomic relation successively only through $T_1,\dots,T_{j-1}$, so each resulting relation reduces a power of $X_i$, $i\le j$, using variables of index at most $i$ and finite words of indices below $i$; repeated Bernstein straightening and the bounded reduction of [F1] therefore never introduce a variable above $j$. In particular $U_j$ is the dot algebra on its first $j$ variables times the finite Hecke algebra. For $1\le k<\ell$ and $h\in U_j$, $\tau(X_{j+1}^kh)=0$, directly from the bounded basis, since the new exponent is positive and bounded. This statement concerns $h\in U_j$, rather than arbitrary $h\in H_n$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

Transferred restricted-profile powers. Write $q=q_H$. For $1\le i\le j+1\le n$, $1\le k\le\ell$ and $h\in U_j$ we claim $\tau(X_{j+1}^kh)=q^{i-j-1}\tau(T_j\cdots T_iX_i^kT_i\cdots T_jh)$, with empty chains when $i=j+1$. The cyclotomic endpoint. Apply step 3.1 with $i=1$, $k=\ell$. In $\tau(q^{-j}T_j\cdots T_1X_1^\ell T_1\cdots T_jh)$ replace $X_1^\ell$ using its first cyclotomic relation. The restriction on $h$ is essential. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

The full Gram blocks. Let $\mathcal B_j$ and $\mathcal C_j$ be the parts of the two bases with entries above $j$ zero, and let $G_j=(\tau(bc))$ be their matrix, of size $N_j=\ell^jn!$. For new profiles $b,c$ at position $j+1$, cyclicity and commuting dots rewrite an entry as $\tau(X_{j+1}^{b+c}hJ_{j+1}^{\delta(c)})$, where $h=X_1^{b_1+c_1}\cdots X_j^{b_j+c_j}T_wT_vJ_1^{\delta(c_1)}\cdots J_j^{\delta(c_j)}\in U_j$ by step 2.2; earlier combined exponents may exceed $\ell-1$, and that same reduction argument is why this remains in $U_j$. Every component-preserving row-standard multitableau factors its distinguished permutation into a permutation inside the contiguous component intervals followed by the unique shuffle of the intervals preserving internal order; the two inversion sets are disjoint, so the factorization is length-additive. Multiplying by $u_\lambda$ (which commutes with the Hecke generators internal to the intervals), ordinary Murphy straightening applies in each component; higher ordinary component shapes preserve component sizes and strictly increase multipartition dominance, and the final component shuffle relabels each component by an increasing list whose selected entries at any cutoff are an initial segment, so tableau-prefix inequalities are exactly the ordinary ones at the corresponding initial-segment length. Right multiplication by $X_1$. Let $t$ be standard with entry $1$ in component $k$, an initial node, and initial label $a+1$ with $a=a_k$. Then $d(t)=(s_a\cdots s_1)w$ with $w$ fixing $1$ and $\ell(d(t))=a+\ell(w)$: pulling label $a+1$ to value $1$ crosses exactly the $a$ smaller initial labels, whose final values exceed $1$. A permutation fixing $1$ has a reduced word in $s_2,\dots,s_{n-1}$, so $T_w$ commutes with $X_1$. Multiplying the identity of step 1.2 on the right by $(T_1\cdots T_a)^{-1}$ and then by $T_w$ gives $m_\lambda T_{d(t)}X_1=q_H^aQ_km_\lambda(T_1\cdots T_a)^{-1}T_w +q_H^ax_\lambda u_b(T_1\cdots T_a)^{-1}T_w,$ whose second term lies in $N^{>\lambda}$ by step 1.2 and finite-generator stability, and whose first term lies modulo $N^{>\lambda}$ in the fixed-initial-row span. Hence that span is stable under $X_1$; multiplying on the left by $T_{d(s)}^*$ and using the left stability of the higher shapes gives the coefficient-independence law $m_{st}h\equiv\sum_vr_{(t,v)}(h)m_{sv}\pmod{N^{>\lambda}}$ first for each generator and then for every word, with coefficients independent of $s$, and $*$ makes the higher spans two-sided. Since $X_r=q_H^{1-r}T_{r-1}\cdots T_1X_1T_1\cdots T_{r-1}$ and the cyclotomic constant term is a unit when the $Q_a$ are invertible, these generators generate the Laurent affine quotient. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

Spanning and cellularity. The smallest multipartition $\omega=(\varnothing,\dots,\varnothing,(1^n))$ satisfies $u_\omega=x_\omega=m_\omega=1$, so the generator-stable span of the standard $m_{st}$ contains $1$ and is all of $H_n$: the Murphy family spans. By [[lem-universal-cyclotomic-hecke-ordered-monomials-form-a-basis]], $H_n$ is independently free of rank $\ell^nn!$. Counting standard pairs with the ordinary identity $\sum_{\rho\vdash m}f_\rho^2=m!$ at the component sizes $n_a$ contributes $(n!)^2/\prod_an_a!$, and summing over the multipartition compositions gives $\ell^nn!$ by the multinomial theorem. The spanning family therefore has exactly the independent rank; its coefficient matrix in the ordered PBW basis is square and surjective between free modules, hence invertible, so the family is an $R$-basis and the proved involution and coefficient-independence laws are actual cellularity. Tensoring the proved basis and presentation supplies every commutative specialization with unit parameters, including repeated charges and the LM deformation DVR; no generic-flatness inference is made. Rank zero is the singleton empty basis. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

Conclusion. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 establish the generator-stable higher ideals for the finite-generator subalgebra; step 2.1 extends stability to $X_1$ and hence to all polynomial generators and gives the coefficient-independence law with two-sided higher spans; and step 3.1 proves that the standard Murphy family is an $R$-basis of exactly the independent rank, so that the involution and coefficient laws are cellularity in the sense of the Definition. Every commutative specialization with unit parameters inherits the basis and the cell law. No primitive-block classification is used. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

proof_steps.text: The affine expansion with only variable-difference denominators. Writing $T_w$ as the product of the $\Phi_i$ and the scalars $c_{i,i+1}$ along a reduced word of $w$ and moving a Laurent polynomial $f$ leftward across the $\Phi$'s by [F2] expresses $T_wf$ as a sum of terms $c_v\,v(f)$ times a monomial in a subword, where $v$ runs over products of subwords of that reduced word, every denominator of $c_v$ is a product of differences $X_i-X_j$, and each $v$ is Bruhat-below $w$ by the subword characterization of Bruhat order ([F6]). In particular applying this with $f=u_\lambda$ keeps all denominators among the variable differences and introduces no $U_a-U_b$, quantum factorial, or Gram determinant. [F1, F2, F6, algebra]

Flagging is Bruhat-downward closed and gives monic divisibility. Let $S$ be semistandard of shape $\lambda$ and type $\mu$, and for a permutation $\sigma$ let $\pi=\sigma^{-1}$ map each label to its physical position; set $A_k=\sum_{a<k}|\lambda^{(a)}|$ and $B_k=\sum_{a<k}|\mu^{(a)}|$. By [F1] the flag condition says that a label of component $a$ occupies only a physical component $b\le a$, i.e. $\#\{r\le B_k:\pi(r)\le A_k\}=B_k$ for all $k$. The count is at most $B_k$; inversion preserves the Bruhat order and a Bruhat-smaller permutation has at least as many entries in every prefix rectangle, so every Bruhat-smaller permutation of a flagged one is flagged. If $\sigma$ is flagged then $\sigma(u_\lambda)=\prod_k\prod_{j\le A_k}(X_{\sigma(j)}-U_k)$ contains the factor $(X_r-U_k)$ for every $r\le B_k$, because $\pi(r)\le A_k$; hence $\sigma(u_\lambda)=u_\mu\prod_j\prod_{a(j)<k\le b(j)}(X_j-U_k)$ with $a(j)$ the physical component of the position occupied by label $j$ and $b(j)$ its type component, a monic polynomial. In particular $u_\mu$ divides $\sigma(u_\lambda)$ in the Laurent polynomial ring. [F1, F6, algebra]

The left row-double-coset identity and localized membership. Let $s_0$ be the least standard refinement of $S$ and $D=S_\mu d(s_0)^{-1}S_\lambda$. Every row-standard refinement of the semistandard $S$ is standard, and the ordinary length-additive left row-double-coset expansion gives $\sum_{s:\,\mu(s)=S}T_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda=\sum_{w\in D}T_w$, each element of $D$ exactly once, with no row-intersection quantum factorial ([F4] proves the identical finite identity; [F1] fixes the elements $T_{d(s)}^*$ and $x_\lambda$). Since $S_\mu$ permutes labels inside $\mu$-components and $S_\lambda$ permutes positions inside $\lambda$-rows, every $w\in D$ is flagged; hence every Bruhat-subword permutation $v$ in the expansion of step 1.1 is flagged by step 1.2, so $v(u_\lambda)=u_\mu g_v$ with $g_v$ a Laurent polynomial, and $T_wu_\lambda\in u_\mu H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}[(X_i-X_j)^{-1}]$ for every $w\in D$. Writing $b_0:=\sum_{w\in D}T_w$ and summing, $b_0u_\lambda\in u_\mu H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}[(X_i-X_j)^{-1}]$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

The flagged span is a right ideal and a left parabolic module. Let $W_\mu$ be the $R$-span of the $m_{st}$ with $s$ $\mu$-flagged. Right multiplication by a finite generator $T_i$ uses the Murphy expansion of [F3]: same-shape terms retain the left tableau, and higher terms arise from ordinary straightening inside physical components whose permutations are products of $d(s)$ with permutations internal to the physical intervals, hence only permute the admissible $\mu$-labels among the nodes of each component; the exact quadratic expansion, row normalization, and straightening inside components preserve the flagged set. Let $M$ be a finite right $H$-module containing $H$ as a direct summand with projection $e$, and $C=\operatorname{End}_H(M)$. Then $eCe=\operatorname{End}_H(H)\cong H$ by left multiplication, and $Ce\cong\operatorname{Hom}_H(H,M)\cong M$ by evaluation at $1$. If $c\in Z(C)$, then $c$ restricts on the $H$-summand to left multiplication by some $h$; for each $m\in M$ the $H$-map $f_m:H\to M$, $a\mapsto ma$, is the off-diagonal block $j f_m\pi\in C$ through $H$, and commuting it with $c$ and evaluating at $1$ gives $c(m)=mh$. Since $c$ is $H$-linear, $c(ab)=c(a)b$ for $a,b\in H$ gives $ab h=ahb$, so with $a=1$ we get $hb=bh$ and $h\in Z(H)$. Conversely every $h\in Z(H)$ defines the $H$-linear endomorphism $m\mapsto mh$, which commutes with every $H$-endomorphism of $M$, hence is central in $C$. These constructions are inverse unital algebra maps, so $Z(C)\cong Z(H)$ and primitive central idempotents correspond bijectively ([F4]). For $M=\bigoplus_\lambda M_\lambda$ we have $M_\omega=H_n$, so this applies with $e=e_\omega$. [F1, F4, algebra]

The unique tableau $T^\lambda$ of shape and type $\lambda$ gives $\varphi_{(T^\lambda,T^\lambda)}=e_\lambda$, the identity projection onto $M_\lambda$, an actual idempotent; evaluating the cell form at $v_{T^\lambda}$ gives $\langle v_{T^\lambda},v_{T^\lambda}\rangle=1$, so every standard is nonzero with nonzero form. Order the multipartitions in a linear extension of dominance and remove the maximal remaining cell layers successively; in the relevant quotient algebra $B$ the next layer $J$ has basis $c_{st}$ with a distinguished index $u$ whose Gram value is $G(u,u)=1$. Then $e=c_{uu}$ is idempotent, $c_{su}c_{ut}=c_{st}$, and the multiplication map $Be\otimes_FeB\to J$ is an isomorphism on these basis elements; also $eBe=Fe$, since the cell law and maximality of $J$ show every $ebe$ is a scalar multiple of $e$. Hence $Be$ is projective, $J$ is a direct sum of copies of $Be$, and $e\,\mathrm{rad}(B)\,e=0$ because the corner is a field. Thus $J$ is a split heredity ideal, and iterating gives a split heredity chain whose standards are the cell modules $\Delta_\lambda$; so $C_n$ is split quasihereditary over $F$. [F2, F3, algebra]

proof_steps.text: Word separation over the universal fraction field. Assign to each standard multitableau the sequence of joint Jucys–Murphy words: the diagonal values $U_az^{j-i}$ at the nodes carrying the labels $1,\dots,n$ ([F3]). If two standard multitableaux first differ at step $r$, then their restrictions to the boxes $1,\dots,r-1$ coincide, and the two added nodes are two different addable nodes of that common prefix shape. If the two nodes lie in one physical component, their contents $j-i$ are different (two addable nodes of a partition have different contents), and $z$ is transcendental over the base field, so $z^{j-i}\ne z^{j'-i'}$. If they lie in different components $a\ne b$, the values $U_az^{j-i}$ and $U_bz^{j'-i'}$ are distinct in $K$, because $z,U_1,\dots,U_\ell$ are algebraically independent monomials and the components differ. Hence the joint word determines the tableau, different standard multitableaux -- even of different shapes -- have different joint words, and distinct shapes have disjoint sets of word characters. [F1, F3, algebra]

Generic simplicity and split semisimplicity. By [F3] each $S_\lambda$ has a simultaneous triangular filtration whose successive characters are its own words of step 1.1. Hence every composition factor $D_\mu$ of the nonzero module $S_\lambda$ has a word occurring in $S_\mu$ and a word occurring in $S_\lambda$; disjointness of shape word sets forces $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $D_\lambda\ne0$, and the cellular diagonal multiplicity $[S_\lambda:D_\lambda]=1$ of [F4] forces $S_\lambda=D_\lambda$ to be simple, with the distinct absolutely simple modules $S_\lambda$ as the only composition factors. The cellular basis gives $\dim_K H_K=\sum_\lambda(\dim_K S_\lambda)^2$. The semisimple quotient is a product of full matrix algebras on the exhaustive absolutely simple $S_\lambda$: to see this, the rank-one cell action on each simple gives every matrix unit, and the distinct simple labels give the distinct simple factors. Its dimension is the same sum, so the radical has dimension zero. Thus $H_K$ is split semisimple; no splitting of the cellular filtration was assumed. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

Word separation for the Lyle–Mathas deformation. Fix $N\ge1$, nonzero $q_H,Q_a$ in $F$, and set $z=q_Ht$, $U_a=Q_at^{Na}$ in $F(t)$. For two standard multitableaux that first differ at a step $r\le N$, the common prefix of size $r-1$ has components of sizes summing to $r-1$; the two added nodes lie in components $a,b$ and each added content $c=j-i$ is bounded in absolute value by the size of its own component, so $|c-c'|<r\le N$. A collision $U_az^c=U_bz^{c'}$ with $a\ne b$ would force the equality $Na+c=Nb+c'$ of $t$-adic exponents, i.e. the nonzero multiple $N(a-b)$ of $N$ would equal $c'-c$ with $|c'-c|<N$, impossible. If $a=b$, then $z$ is transcendental over $F$, so $z^c=z^{c'}$ forces $c=c'$. Thus the joint words separate all rank-$d$ standards in $F(t)$ as in step 1.1, and the argument of step 2.1 proves that the rank-$d$ Specht modules are simple and the corresponding Hecke algebra is split semisimple over $F(t)$, with no affine-center or block-classification input. proof_steps.text: Characters as finite symmetric polynomials. Fix $d\ge n$ row labels per type component with ordered variables $x_{(a,r)}$, put $Y_a=\{x_{(b,r)}:b\ge a\}$ with the inherited order, and for a shape $\lambda$ let $\operatorname{ch}_\lambda(x)=\sum_{T\in\operatorname{SStd}(\lambda)}x^{\operatorname{wt}(T)}$. The flag condition says that the physical component $a$ of a semistandard tableau is an ordinary semistandard tableau over the alphabet $Y_a$, and the components are chosen independently, so $\operatorname{ch}_\lambda(x)=\prod_a s_{\lambda^{(a)}}(Y_a)$ with $s_\rho(Y)=\det(h_{\rho_i-i+j}(Y))$. The determinant equals the ordinary semistandard generating polynomial: expand it as signed families of east/north lattice paths from $(-j,1)$ to $(\rho_i-i,m)$ with east steps at height $r$ weighted $y_r$, choose the first intersection in a fixed order and exchange the two tails, an involution that preserves the monomial weight and reverses the permutation sign, so all intersecting families cancel; a nonintersecting family forces the identity matching, and the surviving families are exactly the semistandard tableaux, sign $+1$. Hence the coefficient of $x^\nu$ in $\operatorname{ch}_\lambda$ is the Kostka number $K_{\lambda\nu}$; empty and short-row cases are included. [F3, F4, F5, algebra]

Beta determinants and rim-hook signs. Choose $N\ge n$, put $\beta_{a,i}=\lambda^{(a)}_i+N-i$ with zero parts appended, and for a nonnegative integer array $v$ define $\chi(v;x)=\prod_a\det\bigl(h_{v_{a,i}-N+j}(Y_a)\bigr)_{i,j}$. If two entries of one component of $v$ agree the determinant has equal rows and is zero; otherwise sorting that component into strictly decreasing order and writing $\rho_i=v'_i-N+i$ gives $\chi(v;x)=\varepsilon(v)\prod_a s_{\rho^{(a)}}(Y_a)$ with $\varepsilon$ the product of the row-sorting signs, so every coefficient is a signed Kostka multiplicity. A beta move lowering a bead from $v+L$ to an unoccupied $v$ is exactly the removal of a rim hook of length $L$: tracing the southeast boundary shows the strip between the two boundary steps has $L$ boxes, its leg is the number of occupied positions strictly between $v$ and $v+L$, its foot content is $v-N+1$, and the associated sorting sign is $(-1)^{\operatorname{leg}}$; the correspondence is a bijection by the reverse move. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

The hook side as a complete finite alternating polynomial. Define $B_\lambda(x)$ as the finite alternating sum of step 2.1: for crosscomponent terms, over $a<b$, over beads $i,j$ and lengths $h\le\beta_{a,i}$, of $\chi(\beta-h e_{a,i}+h e_{b,j};x)V(U_az^{\beta_{a,i}-h}-U_bz^{\beta_{b,j}})$; and for same-component terms, over $a$, $i<j$ and $1\le h\le\beta_{a,i}-\beta_{a,j}-1$, of $\chi(\beta-he_{a,i}+he_{a,j};x)V(U_az^{\beta_{a,i}-h}-U_az^{\beta_{a,j}})$; terms whose $\chi$ is the zero polynomial are omitted before any valuation is evaluated. Then $B_\lambda(x)=\sum_{\mu:\lambda\triangleright\mu}J_{\lambda\mu}\operatorname{ch}_\mu(x)$: a crosscomponent move removing from the earlier component $a$ and adding to a later component $b>a$ produces a strictly dominated $\mu$ and occurs exactly once by the bead description; occupied targets give repeated rows and zero; sorting contributes $(-1)^{\text{removed leg}+\text{added leg}}$; and the prefactor $z^{-N+1}$ converts the beta difference to the difference of the deformed foot residues. In one component the two moved beads $i<j$ give a strict dominance decrease precisely for $1\le h<\beta_i-\beta_j$, the exchange case $h=\beta_i-\beta_j$ giving $\mu=\lambda$ and the outward case giving the reverse dominance; occupied intermediate positions again give zero rows, and the range exceeding a component's size gives a repeated or negative bead, hence a zero determinant. Thus no hook pair is lost or added, and the surviving summands are exactly the $J_{\lambda\mu}$ terms. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

Nonvanishing of every retained foot difference. For a removable rim hook of length $L$ from a partition of size $M+L$ with foot $(h,j)$, one has $-(M+L-1)\le j-h\le M$: every box left of the foot in its row survives, so $j-1\le M$, and $h\le M+L$ gives the lower bound. If $\lambda$ and $\mu$ remove equal-length hooks in distinct components $a\ne b$ to the same remainder with remainder sizes $M_a,M_b$, their foot contents satisfy $|\gamma_x-\gamma_y|\le M_a+M_b+L-1\le n-1$, so the exponent $n(a-b)+\gamma_x-\gamma_y$ is a nonzero integer; in the same component equal foot content and equal length reconstruct the same inverse hook addition, hence would force $\lambda=\mu$, which the strict-dominance terms exclude. Therefore every retained Laurent difference $U_az^u-U_bz^v$ is nonzero in $F(t)$: it is a unit times a nonzero Laurent monomial times $(z^{N}-1)$-type factors and, by [F2], its valuation is finite, being $0$ when the constant residues differ, $1$ in characteristic zero when they agree, and $p^{v_p(N)}$ in characteristic $p$ when they agree. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

The same-component operator. In the same-component beta sum put $D=\beta_i-\beta_j$ and $k=D-h$, so the valuation is $f(k)=V(z^k-1)$ up to unit factors; swapping the two changed determinant rows shows $\chi(\beta-(D-k)e_i+(D-k)e_j;x)=-\chi(\beta-ke_i+ke_j;x)$. Hence the complete coefficient of $f(k)$ is $-\sum_{i<j:\beta_i-\beta_j>k}\chi(\beta-ke_i+ke_j;x)$, which is the strictly dominance-lowering part of $-p_kp_k^\perp$ on the abstract shape basis, where $p_k^\perp$ lowers an occupied bead by $k$ into an unoccupied nonnegative position with sign $(-1)^{\#\text{crossed beads}}$ and $p_k$ raises a bead by $k$ with the same sign rule; the bead-raising formula follows from the alternant identity $\det(y_r^{\beta_i})\sum_ry_r^k=\sum_i\det(y_r^{\beta_i+k\delta_{ij}})$ divided by the Vandermonde, and the removal map is its transpose. After one removal and one addition a non-diagonal lower-dominance result comes only from distinct beads $i<j$ with $0<k<\beta_i-\beta_j$, occupied intermediate positions giving zero repeated rows and the diagonal being removed by the strict projection; this proves the operator identification integrally, in every characteristic. [step 2.1, algebra]

The crosscomponent operator as exterior currents. On the $N$-fold exterior power of a space with basis $e_0,e_1,\dots$, represent a partition by the ordered wedge of its beta beads and let $E(p,q)$ insert $e_p$ after removing $e_q$, with exterior signs; it vanishes if $q$ is absent or $p$ is occupied, and its sign is the bead-sorting sign. Expanding $E=\text{creation}\cdot\text{contraction}$ gives $[E(p,q),E(r,s)]=\delta_{q,r}E(p,s)-\delta_{p,s}E(r,q)$. The crosscomponent matrix acting on column shape vectors is $J^{\mathrm{cross}}=\sum_{a<b}\sum_{h>0}\sum_{q\ge h,w\ge0}V(U_az^{q-h}-U_bz^w)E_a(q,q-h)E_b(w,w+h)$, a finite operator on each size-$n$ sector; the reverse hook pair has forward current $E_a(q-h,q)E_b(w+h,w)$, and transposing gives exactly this operator with the same signs and valuation. [step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, algebra]

Horizontal strips and their conjugation. With $S e_q=e_{q+1}$ and $H(x)=(I-xS)^{-1}=\sum_{r\ge0}x^rS^r$, whose entry $H_{p,q}$ is $x^{p-q}$ for $p\ge q$ and $0$ otherwise, the matrix of $\wedge^NH(x)$ between $\beta_\mu$ and $\beta_\rho$ is $x^{|\mu|-|\rho|}\det(1_{\beta_{\mu,i}\ge\beta_{\rho,j}})$. Subtracting consecutive columns of the $0/1$ matrix makes its determinant $1$ exactly when $\beta_{\mu,i}\ge\beta_{\rho,i}>\beta_{\mu,i+1}$ for all $i$, i.e. $\mu_i\ge\rho_i\ge\mu_{i+1}$, the horizontal-strip criterion, and $0$ otherwise; so $\Gamma(x)=\wedge^NH(x)$ adds every horizontal strip once with weight $x^{\text{strip size}}$. For a type component $a$, $\Gamma_a(x)=\prod_{b\le a}\Gamma_b(x)$ adds a horizontal strip in every permitted physical component $b\le a$ and leaves the rest unchanged, so the successive $\Gamma_a$ from the empty shape enumerate exactly the flagged semistandard tableaux and give the branching matrix. Conjugation is explicit: since $H^{-1}=I-xS$ has column vector $e_p-xe_{p+1}$ and row covector $\sum_{r\le q}x^{q-r}e_r^*$, $\Gamma(x)^{-1}E(p,q)\Gamma(x)=\sum_{r=0}^qx^{q-r}\bigl(E(p,r)-xE(p+1,r)\bigr),$ and the two-current conjugation is the ordered product of two such sums. [step 4.1, algebra]

Strip factors and exact minor expressions. For a permitted strip transition $\rho\to\lambda$ for the next type component $c$, let $\eta=[\lambda]\setminus[\rho]$, $r_x=U_{\operatorname{comp}(x)}z^{\operatorname{content}(x)}$, and put $F^{(c)}_{\lambda\rho}=\prod_{x\in\eta}\prod_{\operatorname{comp}(x)<b\le c}(r_x-U_b)\prod_{x\in[\rho],\,y\in\eta\text{ in one physical row}}C_+(r_x,r_y)\prod_{x<y,\,x,y\in\eta\text{ in different physical rows}}C_+(r_x,r_y)\prod_{x\in\eta,\,y\in[\rho],\,x<y}R(r_x,r_y)$. Splitting the pair lists of [F1] into old/old, old/new and new/new gives this factor, and their product along a semistandard chain is $\gamma_{t_T}/(C_{t_T}u_T)$. Choose $N>n$, write $q_i=\beta_{\lambda,i}$, $p_i=\beta_{\rho,i}$ in each component, and $H(q,p)_{ij}=1_{q_i\ge p_j}$, so $q_N=p_N=0$. Write $\phi(k)=V(z^k-1)$ for $k>0$ and $\psi_{ab}(d)=V(U_az^d-U_b)$. First regard these as independent formal symbols; canceled symbols are never evaluated. By steps 3.1 and 5.1, the same-component row contribution to $J\Gamma$ is $\sum_{i<j}\sum_{0<h<q_i-q_j}\phi(q_i-q_j-h)\det H(q-he_i+he_j,p)$; the column contribution to $\Gamma J$ is $\sum_{i<j}\sum_{h>0}(\phi(p_i-p_j+h)-\phi(h))\det H(q,p+he_i-he_j)$. Negative or repeated shifted beads give zero determinants. For the second formula, the outward source has beads $p_i+h,p_j-h$; its two hook pairs returning to $p$ have lengths $h$ and $p_i-p_j+h$, foot gaps $p_i-p_j+h$ and $h$, and opposite signs because the second pair exchanges the two target beads. This proves the difference of potentials, including crossed inverse sources. A crosscomponent row term replaces $q_{a,i},q_{b,j}$ by $q_{a,i}-h,q_{b,j}+h$ with potential $\psi_{ab}(q_{a,i}-h-q_{b,j})$; its column term replaces $p_{a,i},p_{b,j}$ by $p_{a,i}+h,p_{b,j}-h$ with potential $\psi_{ab}(p_{a,i}-p_{b,j}+h)$. The determinants in the original indexed positions retain all sorting signs. [F1, F6, step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra]

Norm endpoints. On support $q_i\ge p_i>q_{i+1}$. Put $M_i=q_i-p_i$, $K_j=p_j-q_{j+1}-1$ for $j<N$, $K_N=0$, and $S(m)=\sum_{k=1}^m\phi(k)$. The same-component norm valuation is $\sum_i(S(q_i)-S(p_i)-S(M_i))+\sum_{i<j}\sum_{u=p_i}^{q_i-1}(\phi(u-q_j)-\phi(u-p_j+1))$. To verify this directly, put $b_i=N-i$: same-row old/new pairs sum to $S(q_i-b_i)-S(M_i)-S(p_i-b_i)$. For $i<j$, new/new and new-upper/old-lower pairs sum to $\sum_{u=p_i}^{q_i-1}(\phi(u-q_j)-\phi(u-p_j+1)+\phi(u-b_j+1)-\phi(u-b_j))$. The last two terms telescope in $u$ to $\phi(q_i-b_j)-\phi(p_i-b_j)$; summing over $j>i$ cancels the baseline $b_i$ terms and gives the formula. Every displayed $\phi$ argument is positive. For $a<b\le c$, the crosscomponent endpoint expression is $\sum_i\sum_{u=p_{a,i}}^{q_{a,i}-1}(\psi_{ab}(u+1)+\sum_{j=1}^N(\psi_{ab}(u-q_{b,j})-\psi_{ab}(u-p_{b,j}+1)))$. Indeed the new/new $C_+$ factors telescope in the lower-component node index $v$ to $\psi(u-q_{b,j})-\psi(u-p_{b,j})$, and the new/old $R$ factors add $\psi(u-p_{b,j})-\psi(u-b_j)$ and the rectangle difference $\sum_{v=b_j}^{p_{b,j}-1}(\psi(u+1-v)-\psi(u-v))$. Telescoping this rectangle in the other direction and adding the boundary factor $\psi(u-N+1)$ gives the displayed formula; the vacuum differences telescope and cancel that boundary. This padded formula is an equality of formal symbols: its $j=N$ term cancels $\psi(u+1)$ before evaluation. [F1, step 6.1, algebra]

All on-support minors. Here $H$ is the unit upper triangular step matrix. Expanding a replacement row or column in its basis gives $d_i^{\mathrm{row}}(v)=1_{p_i\le v<p_{i-1}}$ and $d_i^{\mathrm{col}}(v)=1_{q_{i+1}<v\le q_i}$, with $p_0=\infty$ and no positive lowering from $p_N=0$. A two-row minor is its direct product minus its crossed product. For the same-component row expression, the direct term has $1\le h\le\min(M_i,K_{j-1})$ and the crossed term, with $k=q_i-q_j-h$, has $1\le k\le\min(M_i,K_{j-1})$. The outward two-column minor has no crossed term and its direct bound is $1\le h\le\min(M_i,K_j)$. Pair direct row index $j+1$ with first-potential column index $j$. For arbitrary symbols $\psi$ the interval identity $\sum_{s=0}^{M-1}(\psi(A+s+K+1)-\psi(A+s+1))=\sum_{h=1}^{\min(M,K)}(\psi(A+M+K+1-h)-\psi(A+h))$ follows by canceling the overlap of the two integer intervals (when $M\le K$ they are disjoint, and when $M>K$ only $K$ endpoints remain). Applying it with $A=p_i-p_j$, the paired contribution is $\sum_{j=i+1}^{N-1}\sum_{u=p_i}^{q_i-1}(\phi(u-q_{j+1})-\phi(u-p_j+1))$. Crossed rows cancel the second column potentials except $-S(\min(M_i,K_i))$; the unpaired direct row $j=i+1$, combined with that residual by the same identity at $A=0$, gives $\sum_{u=p_i}^{q_i-1}\phi(u-q_{i+1})-S(M_i)$. Summing yields exactly the same-component endpoints of step 7.1. For a crosscomponent pair, row $j+1$ and column $j$ share the bound $\min(M_i,K_{b,j})$ and $A=p_{a,i}-p_{b,j}$. The unpaired first row contributes $\sum_{u=p_{a,i}}^{q_{a,i}-1}\psi(u-q_{b,1})$; the final column vanishes. The same interval identity converts the paired terms to the remaining endpoints of step 7.1. Thus $(J\Gamma-\Gamma J)_{\lambda\rho}=x^{|\lambda|-|\rho|}V(F^{(c)}_{\lambda\rho})$ on support. [step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]

Crosscomponent off support. The row of $H$ at bead $v$ is the tail vector starting at threshold $\kappa(v)$, whose interval is $[p_r,p_{r-1})$. Different nonzero tail vectors are independent; hence rank equals the number of distinct thresholds. At rank $N-1$ there is one missing threshold $r$ and two adjacent duplicated rows $i,i+1$. Put $Q=q_i>Q'=q_{i+1}$, $[P,P')=[p_r,p_{r-1})$, $u=e_i-e_{i+1}$ and $v=e_r-e_{r-1}$, omitting $e_0$. The adjugate is $\varepsilon vu^{\mathsf T}$: its nullspaces have those generators, and removing a duplicate row and the appropriate column gives a minor $\pm1$. Thus replacement determinants are $\varepsilon u_l1_{P\le x<P'}$ and $\varepsilon v_l1_{Q'<x\le Q}$ with the same sign. Rank $\le N-2$ kills every one-row/column replacement. A defective earlier component can be repaired only when $Q'\ge P'$ (missing below), and a defective later component only when $Q<P$ (missing above); opposite directions give zero. If only the earlier component is defective, pair normal later row $j+1$ and column $j$ and write $L=q_{b,j+1}$, $M=p_{b,j}$. Their coefficients both give $-\varepsilon\sum_{d\in[P-L,P'-L)\cap(Q'-M,Q-M]}\psi(d)$; the first unpaired row vanishes because its two source signs sum to zero. If only the later component is defective, write its endpoints $R>R'$, $[S,S')$ and let $M=q_{a,i}-p_{a,i}$. The row coefficient at restored position $w$ is $\varepsilon1_{R'+M<w\le R+M}$ on $[S,S')$, and the column coefficient at $t$ is $\varepsilon1_{S\le t+M<S'}$ on $(R',R]$. The translation $w=t+M$ matches their potentials because $q_{a,i}=p_{a,i}+M$. With both components defective, the row coefficient of $\psi(d)$, divided by $\varepsilon_a\varepsilon_b$, is $(1_{S\le Q-d<S'}-1_{S\le Q'-d<S'})(1_{P\le R+d<P'}-1_{P\le R'+d<P'})$; the column coefficient is $(1_{R'<P-d\le R}-1_{R'<P'-d\le R})(1_{Q'<S+d\le Q}-1_{Q'<S'+d\le Q})$. They agree by the endpoint identity $1_{B_0\le A_1-d<B_1}-1_{B_0\le A_0-d<B_1}=1_{A_0<B_0+d\le A_1}-1_{A_0<B_1+d\le A_1}$, obtained by regrouping four half-line indicators. Infinite top endpoints simply omit the virtual source. An untouched defective component kills the product. Components beyond $c$ are empty in the reachable prefix: the forward transfer would create a nonempty forbidden intermediate component, and the inverse transfer would remove a hook from an empty component, so both vanish. This exhausts crosscomponent off-support cases. [step 6.1, step 8.1, algebra]

Same-component deficiency one, missing below. Keep the rank-one data of step 9.1, with duplicated rows $s,s+1$ and missing threshold $r>s$, so $Q'\ge P'$. A nonzero inward two-row replacement must use one duplicate source and a unique normal row $j\ge r+1$: one new row fills the missing interval and the other restores the unique source threshold. The direct and exchanged assignments have signs $\varepsilon u_l$ and $-\varepsilon u_l$; any other assignment leaves an unchanged duplicate or missing threshold, or violates the strict inward range. Nonzero outward two-column repairs use one endpoint $P,P'$ and a unique column $j\ge r+1$, or the endpoint pair itself. Put $K_j=p_j-q_{j+1}-1$ for $j\ge r$, $K_N=0$. The direct row contribution is $R_j=-\varepsilon\sum_{d\in[P-q_j,P'-q_j)\cap(Q'-p_{j-1},Q-p_{j-1}]}\phi(d)$. Split each unique column contribution into its first and second potentials $C_j^{\mathrm{first}}-C_j^{\mathrm{second}}$ from step 6.1. Then $R_{j+1}=C_j^{\mathrm{first}}$, by the same interval intersection, while $C_j^{\mathrm{second}}=\varepsilon\sum_{h=1}^{K_j}\phi(h)(1_{Q'<P+h\le Q}-1_{Q'<P'+h\le Q})$. The exchanged row is $X_j=-\varepsilon\sum_{k=1}^{K_{j-1}}\phi(k)(1_{P\le Q-k<P'}-1_{P\le Q'-k<P'})=-C_{j-1}^{\mathrm{second}}$ by endpoint reciprocity. All terms cancel except $R_{r+1}-C_r^{\mathrm{second}}-C^{\mathrm{end}}$. Put $A=Q'-P'\ge0$, $B=P'-P>0$, $L=Q-Q'>0$, $I_0=(A,A+L]$, $I_1=I_0+B$, $K=K_r$. These three terms are respectively $-\varepsilon\sum_{d\in I_1\cap(K,K+B]}\phi(d)$, $\varepsilon\sum_{h=1}^{K}\phi(h)(1_{I_1}(h)-1_{I_0}(h))$, and $-\varepsilon\sum_{h\in I_0,\,1\le h\le K}(\phi(B+h)-\phi(h))$; the endpoint-pair sign is negative because the raised endpoint is $P'$. Their residual is $-\varepsilon\sum_{d\in I_1\cap[1,K+B]}\phi(d)+\varepsilon\sum_{h\in I_0,\,1\le h\le K}\phi(B+h)=0$ by $d=h+B$. This proves every coefficient cancels, including $K=0$. [step 6.1, step 9.1, algebra]

Same-component deficiency one, missing above. Here $r\le s$, $P>Q$, and $\varepsilon=(-1)^{s-r}$, obtained by moving the inserted missing threshold from row $s$ to position $r$; the column cofactor has the same sign. If $r=1$, all inward row positions are at most $q_1<p_1$ and cannot fill the missing top threshold; the first column is zero and any outward repair raises it further, so both sums vanish. For $r\ge2$ the only unique row sources are $i\le r-1$, with $M_i=q_i-p_i\ge0$. The direct rows have $R_i=\varepsilon\sum_{d\in(q_i-P',q_i-P]\cap[p_i-Q,p_i-Q')}\phi(d)$. The first column potentials equal $R_i$ for $i\le r-2$, while $C_i^{\mathrm{second}}=\varepsilon\sum_{h=1}^{M_i}\phi(h)(1_{Q'<P-h\le Q}-1_{Q'<P'-h\le Q})$. Exchanged rows are $X_i=-\varepsilon\sum_{k=1}^{M_i}\phi(k)(1_{P\le Q+k<P'}-1_{P\le Q'+k<P'})=-C_i^{\mathrm{second}}$, again by endpoint reciprocity. This exhausts repairs: the duplicate source must be paired with a head row above the missing interval, and outward column repairs must lower an endpoint paired with a unique head column, or use the endpoint pair. The sole residual is at $i=r-1$. Put $M=q_{r-1}-P'\ge0$, $B=P'-P>0$, $A=P-Q>0$, $L=Q-Q'>0$, $I_0=[A,A+L)$, $I_1=I_0+B$. Then $R_{r-1}=\varepsilon\sum_{d\in I_1\cap(M,M+B]}\phi(d)$ and $C_{r-1}^{\mathrm{second}}=\varepsilon\sum_{h=1}^M\phi(h)(1_{I_0}(h)-1_{I_1}(h))$; the endpoint-pair column term is $C^{\mathrm{end}}=\varepsilon\sum_{h\in I_0,\,1\le h\le M}(\phi(B+h)-\phi(h))$, with positive cofactor because the lowered endpoint is $P$. Thus $R_{r-1}-C_{r-1}^{\mathrm{second}}-C^{\mathrm{end}}=\varepsilon\sum_{d\in I_1\cap[1,M+B]}\phi(d)-\varepsilon\sum_{h\in I_0,\,1\le h\le M}\phi(B+h)=0$. The translation $d=h+B$ is valid since $A>0$. [step 6.1, step 9.1, algebra]

Same-component deficiency two and higher. At rank $N-2$, the excess threshold copies are one triple or two pairs. Inward row repairs of a triple cannot reach missing thresholds between its source beads. For two pairs with thresholds $r<s$, both missing thresholds must lie strictly between them, say $r<m_1<m_2<s$; otherwise both row and column sums are zero. For columns this follows from $\ell(p_j)=\#\{i:\kappa(q_i)\le j\}$: duplicated row thresholds are jumps, missing thresholds are flats, and outward column repairs require two separate size-two jumps with both flats between. A zero first column also cannot be repaired by raising it. In the active pattern put $Q=q_r>Q'=q_{r+1}$, $R=q_{s-1}>R'=q_s$, $I_1=[P,P')=[p_{m_1},p_{m_1-1})$, $I_2=[S,S')=[p_{m_2},p_{m_2-1})$, $J_Q=(Q',Q]$, $J_R=(R',R]$. The common row/column sign is $\varepsilon=(-1)^{m_1-r+s-1-m_2}$, counted by moving the inserted thresholds to their sorted positions. Switching a source copy or switching the two target thresholds reverses it. Define $A_I(k)=1_{R+k\in I}-1_{R'+k\in I}$ and $B_I(k)=1_{Q-k\in I}-1_{Q'-k\in I}$; define $D_P^\pm(J;k)=1_{P\pm k\in J}-1_{P'\pm k\in J}$ and $D_S^\pm(J;k)=1_{S\pm k\in J}-1_{S'\pm k\in J}$. The complete row coefficient of $\phi(k)$ is $\varepsilon(A_{I_1}(k)B_{I_2}(k)-A_{I_2}(k)B_{I_1}(k))$; the column coefficient is $\varepsilon(D_S^+(J_Q;k)D_P^-(J_R;k)-D_P^+(J_Q;k)D_S^-(J_R;k))$. Indeed putting $k=q_i-q_j-h$ gives row targets $q_j+k,q_i-k$, while the positive and negative column potentials give targets $p_j+k,p_i-k$ and $p_i+k,p_j-k$ respectively. Interval membership implies all required positive-length bounds. Endpoint reciprocity gives $A_{I_1}=D_P^-(J_R)$, $A_{I_2}=D_S^-(J_R)$, $B_{I_1}=D_P^+(J_Q)$, $B_{I_2}=D_S^+(J_Q)$, proving equality. If $m_2=m_1+1$, the repeated column groups share an endpoint; its formal double-source term is zero because its potential is $\phi(h)-\phi(h)$, so the formula still includes adjacent missing thresholds. At rank $\le N-3$, two replacements cannot restore full rank. Together with steps 9.1–10.2 this proves off-support vanishing for every rank and orientation. All identities are formal coefficient equalities; retained terms are actual valid hook currents, so step 3.2 permits their finite arbitrary-characteristic valuation specialization. [step 6.1, step 9.1, step 10.1, step 10.2, algebra]

Telescoping and the valuation formula. Multiply the $\Gamma$ matrices in increasing type-row-label order and telescope $J\Gamma-\Gamma J$ from $J_0=0$; by steps 8.1–11.1 each commutator inserts exactly $V(F)$ at its strip position, so the $\lambda$-coordinate of the resulting identity is $\sum_T V(\gamma_{t_T}/(C_{t_T}u_T))x^{\operatorname{wt}(T)}=L_\lambda(x)$ on one side and $B_\lambda(x)$ on the other. All padded artificial symbols cancel before the surviving coefficients are evaluated, and every surviving coefficient corresponds to a valid current, hence by step 3.2 to a nonzero foot difference with finite valuation. Comparing with the exact monic product [F1] and the hook side of step 3.1, and taking the coefficient of $x^
u$ at an actual multipartition weight $
u$ (auxiliary compositions only index the same polynomials and never enter the Schur conclusion), gives $V(\det G_{\lambda
u})=\sum_\mu J_{\lambda\mu}K_{\mu
u};$ the empty case $n=0$ gives $0$, all ranks keep the fixed parameters $z=q_Ht$, $U_a=Q_at^{na}$, and arbitrary-composition coefficients are combinatorial only. [F1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 8.1, step 11.1, algebra] ∎
